summary:
Astro Health Monitor is a full-stack web application I developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. The goal was to explore how technology could help astronauts keep track of their health during long-duration space missions.

The application provides a dashboard that displays simulated vital signs, including heart rate, body temperature, and blood oxygen levels (SpO₂). I also integrated **A.R.V.I.N**, an AI-powered assistant built using Google's Gemini API, allowing astronauts to ask questions and receive responses through a simple chat interface.

I built the application using React, Node.js, Express, and PostgreSQL, with a secure login system that allows crew members to access their dashboard using their own accounts.

Monitoring astronaut health is especially important during space missions, where immediate medical assistance may not always be available. While the current version uses simulated health data, the project demonstrates how health monitoring and AI assistance could work together in a single platform, with the potential to support real sensor data in the future.
details:
Project Details

What is Astro Health Monitor?

Astro Health Monitor is a full-stack web application I developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. The idea behind the project was to explore how astronauts could monitor their health and access AI assistance during space missions through a single, easy-to-use platform.

Space missions can be physically demanding, and astronauts may not always have immediate access to medical professionals. I wanted to explore how a digital health monitoring system could make important information more accessible to crew members.

How Does It Work?

The application has three main components.

1. Crew Authentication

Astronauts can register using a unique Crew ID and password, then log in to access their personal dashboard. The backend handles authentication using JWT tokens stored in HTTP-only cookies, while passwords are securely hashed using bcrypt.

2. Health Monitoring Dashboard

Once logged in, crew members can view three health indicators:

  • Heart rate (BPM)
  • Body temperature (°C)
  • Blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂)

The readings update automatically to demonstrate how a live health monitoring interface could function. Currently, the data is simulated rather than collected from physical sensors.

3. A.R.V.I.N — AI Assistant

One of the main features I developed is A.R.V.I.N, an AI assistant powered by Google's Gemini API.

A.R.V.I.N provides a conversational interface where astronauts can ask questions and receive AI-generated responses. I wanted the assistant to feel like a natural part of the dashboard rather than a separate tool.

Technologies Used

I developed the frontend using React, Vite, React Router, and CSS.

For the backend, I used Node.js and Express.js to handle API requests, authentication, and communication with the Gemini API.

PostgreSQL, hosted on Neon, stores crew account information. The application is deployed using Vercel.

The project is entirely software-based and does not currently require external monitoring hardware.

What Makes It Different?

My main focus was bringing health monitoring, crew authentication, and AI assistance together in one application.

Rather than building a static dashboard, I wanted users to interact with the system, create their own accounts, observe changing health readings, and communicate with A.R.V.I.N.
